stories.label: Iran activates air defences as Trump faces war powers deadline in Congress
stories.summary: Tehran briefly activated air defences against drones and small aircraft Thursday night while the White House signalled it will not let Congress rein in war authorisation. Lead with the air-defence activation as the concrete new development on the war-powers arc — yesterday's coverage focused on the procedural deadline; today the war is materialising in Iranian skies. Reader gets the mechanism by which executive war-making bypasses legislative checks even as the conflict escalates.

stories.label: Palestine Action defendants dismiss lawyers to address jury directly
stories.summary: Pro-Palestine activists in a UK criminal trial dismissed their lawyers to address the jury themselves about Britain's role in Gaza. The angle: a rare procedural move that turns a property-damage prosecution into a public forum on UK arms exports and complicity. Lead with the courtroom mechanic — defendants weighed the trade-off and chose direct testimony over legal protection. Reader gets a concrete instance of how speech-restricted political defendants are using trial procedure itself as a platform.

stories.label: A Growing Rat Infestation Plagues Tent Cities in Gaza
stories.summary: Gaza City's preventive health chief: 'We are suffering from two wars — the war of bombs, and the war of rats.' The angle: rodent-borne disease is becoming a second front in the displacement camps as sanitation collapses. Lead with the health official's quote, then the mechanism — destroyed waste infrastructure plus tent density plus blocked aid creates the conditions for an epidemiological crisis on top of the kinetic one. Continuation of siege IS the development.

stories.label: US Deep-Sea Mining Policy Is Eroding Its Pacific Partnerships
stories.summary: Washington's unilateral push for seabed mining licences in the Pacific is alienating the island states it depends on for forward basing and deterrence. Lead with the trade-off: short-term mineral access for long-term loss of Pacific partnerships that took decades to build. Reader gets the strategic mechanism — extractive policy and security architecture are colliding in the same ocean. Addresses the Oceania coverage gap flagged in the audit.

stories.label: Africa embraces China's zero-tariff policy
stories.summary: China cleared its first import shipment under an expanded zero-tariff policy covering all least-developed African countries — a concrete trade-policy contrast with US tariff escalation. Sources span Beijing, Kuala Lumpur, Nairobi and Johannesburg, so coverage frames this as African policy uptake, not Chinese announcement. Lead with the first-shipment-cleared milestone and the country list, then the strategic angle: zero-tariff access is a counter-positioning move while Washington raises trade walls. Note the obvious caveat — China Daily is a state outlet — but the trade flows are verifiable and African outlets are reporting it as a real opening.

stories.label: Santa Marta: Key outcomes from first summit on 'transitioning away' from fossil fuels
stories.summary: The first ministerial summit dedicated to operationalising the COP28 'transition away' language closed in Santa Marta with a non-binding declaration, no production cap, and no finance mechanism for affected workers. Lead with what was NOT agreed — the absence is the story, given the summit's stated purpose. Reader gets the mechanism gap: language adopted at COP without enforcement architecture remains an aspirational signal, even three years on. Pairs with the China Briefing fossil-controls coverage from yesterday.

stories.label: Two disasters in Brazil show climate aid must account for gender and age
stories.summary: Field research from two Brazilian climate disasters — Rio Grande do Sul floods and the Amazon drought — finds aid distribution systematically missed elderly women and child-headed households. Lead with the demographic finding, then the operational mechanism: registration systems that assume adult male heads of household route aid past the most vulnerable. Reader gets a concrete failure mode in disaster response that generalises to every climate-amplified disaster zone, including Pakistan and Bangladesh. Addresses the Latin America sub-regional gap.

stories.label: Congress punts FISA renewal to June
stories.summary: Congress kicked Section 702 reauthorisation to June without resolving the warrant requirement for US-person queries — meaning the FBI will continue running backdoor searches under existing rules through the deadline. Lead with the procedural punt and what it means operationally: the surveillance machinery does not pause when the legislative calendar slips. Reader gets the mechanism by which 'temporary' surveillance authorities ratchet permanent through repeated short-term extensions.

stories.label: The Chinese lesson on the human rights approach to AI
stories.summary: China's AI governance — algorithm filings, generative-content rules, deepfake labelling — has produced a concrete enforcement regime even as Western 'AI ethics' debates remain advisory. Lead with the inversion: the authoritarian state is operating a denser AI rulebook than the democracies preaching rights frameworks, and Global South regulators are studying which model to copy. Reader gets the comparative-governance angle without endorsing either system — it's the regulatory mechanism, not the politics, that's worth understanding.

stories.label: Zed 1.0
stories.summary: Rust-based collaborative code editor Zed shipped 1.0 — a from-scratch GPU-rendered editor competing in a category long owned by Microsoft VS Code. Lead with the technical bet: native Rust, GPU rendering, real-time collaboration as a primitive, and what that means for editor performance on large codebases. Reader is the developer who has watched the editor space stagnate around Electron — this is a credible alternative reaching stable.

stories.label: Oil prices touched their highest level in 4 years. What does it mean for shoppers?
stories.summary: Brent has hit a 4-year high as the Iran war and Hormuz uncertainty bid up the barrel — and US retail diesel/gasoline pass-through is starting to land. The angle: this is the macro receipt for the Khamenei-Strait story; one news cycle, two sides of the same chokepoint shock. Lead with the price level and the specific consumer items already moving (diesel → trucking → grocery). Tie back to the Pentagon's $25B Iran-war cost figure on the ledger.

stories.label: InSight Crime's 2025 Cocaine Seizure Round-Up
stories.summary: InSight Crime's annual seizure tally maps where cocaine was intercepted in 2025 — and the geography has shifted decisively from the Caribbean to West African and European Atlantic ports. The angle: seizure data is the only public proxy for the trade itself, and the redirect through Senegal/Guinea-Bissau/Spain reveals where the new corridors run. Lead with the largest single seizures and the country shifts, then the implication for African coastal states becoming transshipment hubs.

stories.label: Not a lack of cases, but a lack of will: Just 2 verdicts in over a decade of discrimination lawsuits
stories.summary: Egypt's anti-discrimination statute, on the books for over a decade, has produced just two verdicts — Mada Masr's investigation traces the cases that were filed, dropped, or stalled. The angle: this is a structural accountability gap, not an absence of complaints. Lead with the 2-verdicts-in-a-decade number, then explain the prosecutorial discretion that buries the rest. Reader gets a mechanism for how legal protections become symbolic without enforcement.

stories.label: An old railroad is key to U.S.-China race for critical metals in Africa
stories.summary: The Lobito Corridor — a colonial-era railway from Angola's Atlantic port through DRC's copperbelt — is being rebuilt with US backing as Washington's bid to break China's outbound logistics monopoly on African critical metals. The angle: the Lobito vs Tazara (China's east-coast line) rivalry is the physical infrastructure layer of the EV-supply-chain contest. Lead with the corridor's geography and the cobalt/copper tonnage at stake, then how African states play both sides. Pairs with the Central Asia minerals arc on the ledger.

stories.label: Coupang probe tests the U.S.'s willingness to protect its tech giants abroad
stories.summary: South Korean regulators are investigating Coupang — majority-owned by US-listed Coupang Inc. — over a data breach, and US Congress is being asked whether to treat foreign regulatory pressure on a US-listed firm as a trade issue. The angle: this is the inverse of the TikTok playbook. Lead with the ownership structure and the breach, then the precedent question of when a US-listed company's foreign subsidiary becomes a State Department file. Reader gets the mechanism by which 'national champion' arguments cut both ways.

stories.label: After Supreme Court Decision, Louisiana Weighs Redrawing House Maps
stories.summary: SCOTUS ruled Louisiana's congressional map unconstitutional, forcing Gov. Landry to consider postponing the May 16 primary and redrawing districts mid-cycle. Lead with the Voting Rights Act precedent — this is the first major test of the post-2025 VRA framework, and other states with challenged maps will follow. Reader is asking: what does federal voting protection still mean when SCOTUS keeps narrowing it?

stories.label: How the Dreams of Bangladesh's Student Protestors Died Young
stories.summary: Two years after Bangladesh's July 2024 uprising toppled Sheikh Hasina, the student foot soldiers who led it are being marginalized, jailed, or killed by the very interim order they installed. Lead with what 'revolution eats its own' looks like in concrete cases — names, charges, fates. The mechanism: when students dismantle a regime without building durable political institutions, the next set of elites captures the vacuum.

stories.label: The Uncertain Future of America's Afghan Allies
stories.summary: The Trump administration is folding Afghan SIV holders — interpreters, contractors, and their families promised US asylum — into a Congo minerals deal, sending them to Kinshasa instead of the US. Lead with the precedent: outsourcing asylum to a third country in exchange for cobalt and copper access. Protests in Kinshasa show the receiving country didn't fully consent either. The reader needs to see this as a template — refugee obligations as bargaining chip in resource diplomacy.

stories.label: The US will suffer more from oil shock than China, Russia, or EU
stories.summary: EIA data through April 24 shows a 6.2 million barrel drawdown of US oil inventories as tankers reroute to Asia where prices are higher. Average US gasoline jumped from $3.03/gal (Feb) → $3.77 (Mar) → $4.24 (Apr). Lead with the counterintuitive mechanism: the US is the world's biggest oil producer and consumes 2x more oil per dollar of GDP than the EU, so the Hormuz shock hits American consumers harder than it hits China, Russia, or the EU. The 'we're energy independent' political claim collides with how a global commodity market actually works. Frame as economic analysis, not advocacy.

stories.label: US-Indian space mission maps extreme subsidence in Mexico City
stories.summary: NISAR — the joint NASA-ISRO synthetic aperture radar satellite — has produced its first major dataset, mapping centimeter-scale ground subsidence under Mexico City through clouds and vegetation that block optical sensors. Lead with what's new: real-time, all-weather radar coverage of every city on Earth at this resolution did not exist until now. The structural angle: groundwater extraction is sinking Mexico City fast enough to read from orbit, and the same instrument will now expose subsidence in Jakarta, Tehran, Lagos, Dhaka.

stories.label: China Briefing 30 April 2026: Fossil fuel 'strict controls' | El Niño approaches | Why cleantech exports have surged
stories.summary: Beijing has just placed 'strict controls' on new fossil fuel approvals while cleantech exports — solar modules, EVs, batteries — surged again. Lead with the policy pivot: the same week it tightened domestic coal/gas, China shipped record cleantech to the Global South, including Pakistan, Indonesia, Egypt. The structural angle: China is decoupling its growth from oil precisely while US gasoline prices spike from the Hormuz shock. The two trajectories are diverging, and Muslim-world buyers are choosing the cheaper, lower-carbon supplier.

stories.label: The hidden costs of Asia's data center rush
stories.summary: Hyperscale AI data centers are landing across Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines — countries with no environmental impact assessment requirement and regulatory frameworks years behind the build pace. Lead with what local communities don't get to see: water draws, grid loadshedding, land conversions, none of it disclosed. The accountability angle: the AI compute the West uses is being fed by infrastructure that wouldn't be permitted in the US or EU, sited in the Global South for that reason. Reader is a developer who calls these APIs daily — they need the cost on the other end.

stories.label: Stock market holiday today: Are NSE, BSE, MCX open or closed on May 1?
stories.summary:
[Auto-backfill for economy floor] If you are planning to trade today, the Indian stock market will remain shut on May 1 on account of Maharashtra Day and Labour Day.

Both the Bombay Stock Exchange and the National Stock Exchange are closed for trading across segments, as per the official holiday calendar.

There will be no trading

stories.label: Supreme Leader Says Iran Is Planning for Ongoing Control of Strait
stories.summary: Khamenei has signalled Iran intends indefinite control of Strait of Hormuz shipping — telling the US its 'only place in the Persian Gulf is at the bottom of its waters'. The angle: this reframes the Iran war from a transient strike-and-counterstrike into a structural seizure of a chokepoint that carries ~20% of global oil. Lead with the Khamenei quote, then explain what 'ongoing control' means for tanker traffic and insurance markets. Pairs with today's oil-price story.

stories.label: Iran accuses Israel of 'piracy' for seizure of Gaza aid flotilla
stories.summary: Israel intercepted the Sumud aid flotilla in international waters off Crete, detaining crew including three journalists; Iran is calling it piracy and RSF is demanding the journalists' release. The angle: the legal status of the seizure (international waters, not Israeli) and the targeting of accredited journalists alongside aid workers. Lead with the location and the journalists, then the diplomatic fallout. Symmetric dignity: name the detained.

stories.label: After Seven Years, First U.S. Direct Flight Lands in Caracas
stories.summary: American Airlines just landed the first scheduled US-Venezuela commercial flight in seven years, ending a Maduro-era suspension. The angle: a quiet de facto normalisation under Trump that contradicts the simultaneous regime-change posture from Washington hawks. Lead with the flight number and the Miami-Caracas symbolism, then the contradiction with sanctions still in place. Latin America is too often a setting — here Venezuela is the actor reopening.

stories.label: Former Kyrgyz Security Chief Charged With Coup-plotting and Abuse of Office
stories.summary: Kyrgyzstan's former GKNB security chief has been charged with plotting a coup against President Japarov — a case that fits the Central Asian pattern of post-handover purges of the previous regime's security apparatus. The angle: this is how Japarov consolidates, framed as anti-corruption. Lead with the office (intelligence chief), the charge, and the broader pattern of Central Asian leaders using coup-plotting indictments to neutralise rivals. Fills today's chronic Central Asia gap.

stories.label: Roblox Shares Tumble After User Numbers Fall Short
stories.summary: Roblox slashed its annual bookings forecast and the stock dropped after new child-safety features dragged user numbers down — Reuters and Bloomberg both flag the safety/growth tradeoff. The angle: regulatory and reputational pressure (post-Flock/CSAM scrutiny of platforms hosting minors) is now showing up directly in the financials of the largest minor-facing platform. Lead with the bookings cut, then the safety features that caused it. Mechanism: when you can't monetise an underage user, the unit economics shift.

stories.label: A longstanding quantum roadblock just fell, opening existing fiber networks to ultra-secure light signals
stories.summary: Researchers have demonstrated that quantum key distribution can travel over standard telecom fiber alongside classical traffic — removing the dedicated-fiber barrier that has kept QKD a lab toy. The angle: this is the engineering step that turns quantum-secure communication from infrastructure-replacement into infrastructure-overlay. Lead with what just changed (co-existence on existing fiber), then why the cost-deployment math now shifts. Reader is technically literate and will grasp the difference between 'theoretical possibility' and 'deploy-on-Tuesday'.

stories.label: Researchers try to cut the genetic code from 20 to 19 amino acids
stories.summary: A lab has engineered E. coli to live without isoleucine — knocking the universal genetic code from 20 amino acids to 19 — and the surviving cells then become a chassis where the freed codon can encode something synthetic. The angle: this is a foundational step toward organisms that natural viruses and horizontal gene transfer cannot infect, because the code itself no longer matches. Lead with the dropped amino acid and the freed codon, then the biocontainment / synthetic-biology implication.

stories.label: As the most severe Linux threat in years surfaces, the world scrambles
stories.summary: A kernel-level Linux privilege-escalation vulnerability is being patched globally; cloud providers and CI infrastructure are exposed because the bug lives in the kernel path used by container escapes. The angle: virtually every public-cloud workload runs on the affected kernel. Lead with the CVE class (privilege escalation in kernel), then the blast radius (containers → host → tenant). Reader is technical enough to want the mechanism, not just the panic level.

stories.label: Pivotal US-Iran war deadline approaches with no end in sight for conflict
stories.summary: Trump faces a Friday War Powers Resolution deadline to either end the Iran war or formally ask Congress to extend it — and the deadline will pass with neither happening. Lead with the constitutional mechanism: a 1973 law written to stop another Vietnam is being ignored in real time, and the conflict has frozen into a standoff over Gulf shipping. Tie to the Pentagon's $25B cost figure already on the ledger. Reader should grasp that 'no end in sight' means the executive has effectively chosen indefinite war without legislative cover.

stories.label: Moscow's 9 May parade to be held without military equipment
stories.summary: For the first time in decades, Red Square's Victory Day parade will roll without tanks or heavy military vehicles — Russia simply does not have the spare equipment. Lead with the absence as the story: the parade is choreographed power, and the missing armor is a visible accounting of what Ukraine has destroyed. Frame this as battlefield arithmetic the Kremlin can no longer hide from its own public.

stories.label: U.S., Iran remain deadlocked over blockade; Lebanese aid workers killed in Israeli “double tap”; Over half of South Sudan’s population faces acute hunger
stories.summary: Lead with the named tactic: an Israeli 'double tap' strike — a second missile timed to hit first responders — killed Lebanese aid workers responding to an initial strike. The double-tap is a war-crime pattern documented in Syria and Yemen, and it is now a Lebanese reality. Pair with the South Sudan figure: more than half the population faces acute hunger. The reader needs to see two enforcement gaps in one cycle — Lebanon's UN ceasefire mechanism and Sudan's stalled famine response — both ignored.

stories.label: 17 Sudanese refugees drown off Tobruk, Libya - Dabanga Radio TV Online
stories.summary: UNHCR confirms 17 Sudanese refugees drowned off Tobruk after a 33-person boat capsized; only seven survived. Lead with the route, not the count: Sudanese fleeing the RSF-SAF war are now reaching Libya's eastern coast — 1,800km from Khartoum — because the Egyptian land border has tightened and the central Mediterranean route from western Libya is saturated. The displacement is pushing further along the African coast. Names the actor (UNHCR), the victims, and the structural shift in smuggling geography.

stories.label: Who Is ‘El Jardinero,’ the CJNG Power Broker Arrested in Mexico?
stories.summary: Two months after CJNG's leader was killed, Mexican forces have captured 'El Jardinero,' the cartel's senior power broker — and the second-tier of Mexico's most formidable criminal network is now decapitated. Lead with the succession question: CJNG's strength has been its disciplined hierarchy, and removing the bench in 60 days tests whether the network fragments into rival cells (raising violence) or consolidates under a new face (preserving the franchise). The reader should understand this as an organizational stress test, not just an arrest.

stories.label: Ireland 'buffered' against higher inflation - economist
stories.summary: The ECB held rates today and signaled a possible June hike — directly because the Iran war is feeding through Gulf shipping disruption into eurozone inflation. Lead with the transmission mechanism: a war over the Strait of Hormuz is now setting the price of money in Frankfurt. Ireland's 'buffer' is the framing hook (smaller open economy, less direct exposure), but the larger story is that European monetary policy has lost autonomy from Middle East kinetics. Multi-source view from IE/US/IN sharpens the global angle.

stories.label: Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi moved to house arrest, state media says
stories.summary: Five years after the coup, the junta has moved Aung San Suu Kyi from prison to house arrest — a calibrated softening, not a release. Lead with the timing: the junta is preparing for sham elections later this year and needs international optics to unlock frozen aid and sanctions relief. The reader should see this as economic engineering through political theater. Multi-source: Reuters/Al Jazeera/Hindustan Times gives the wire fact, the Muslim-world frame (Rohingya), and the Indian neighbor view.

stories.label: From debt we came, to debt we shall return: New borrowing makes up half of resources in govt’s draft budget
stories.summary: Egypt's draft FY budget shows new borrowing accounts for over half of total resources — and 64% of all spending goes to debt service. Lead with the two numbers: the government is borrowing to pay interest on prior borrowing. This is the textbook signature of a sovereign approaching debt-trap territory. Reader should grasp that IMF program 'success' has stabilized the currency while leaving the underlying fiscal arithmetic unchanged. Egypt's case is the most acute test of the post-2022 EM debt cycle.

stories.label: City Learns Flock Accessed Cameras in Children's Gymnastics Room as a Sales Pitch Demo, Renews Contract Anyway
stories.summary: Dunwoody, Georgia learned that Flock — the surveillance vendor it pays for license-plate readers — accessed live feeds from a children's gymnastics room as part of a sales demo. The city renewed the contract anyway. Lead with the demo: a private company browsed cameras inside a kids' facility to win business, and the elected response was to keep paying. Reader should see the structural failure — Flock's nationwide camera network has no meaningful access controls, and municipal procurement does not treat that as disqualifying. The Fourth Amendment was not designed to be enforced by a city council.

stories.label: J. Craig Venter, Scientist Who Decoded the Human Genome, Dies at 79
stories.summary: Venter's death at 79 closes the chapter on the most consequential outsider in modern biology — the private scientist who forced the public Human Genome Project to finish years ahead of schedule by racing it. Lead with the race itself: in 2000 Bill Clinton brokered a tie, but the competition is what compressed a 15-year plan into a 3-year sprint and built the cost curve that now lets a genome be sequenced for $200. The reader should see Venter as the case study for when controversy and competition accelerate science rather than corrupting it.

stories.label: Massive reef expansion 20 million years ago may explain modern coral life's origins
stories.summary: New work in Science Advances dates the largest coral reef expansion in 100 million years to 20–10 million years ago, between Australia and Southeast Asia — and identifies that window as the cradle of every modern reef ecosystem. Lead with the geographic origin: today's Coral Triangle is biodiverse because that's where reefs survived and seeded the planet. The reader should connect this to current bleaching: the same triangle is now the warmest, most stressed reef zone on Earth — losing the place where coral life began.

stories.label: Microsoft open-sources "the earliest DOS source code discovered to date"
stories.summary: Microsoft has released the earliest known 86-DOS source code — predating the version it bought from Seattle Computer Products in 1981 and built MS-DOS on. Lead with the provenance question: what's in the archive is the operating system whose acquisition turned a small Albuquerque company into the platform owner of the PC era. Reader gets the historical document and the strategic lesson: the most lucrative software deal of the 20th century was the rights to a $50,000 codebase. Show the ingredient.

stories.label: Japan Is Building Cardboard Suicide Drones
stories.summary: AirKamuy, a Japanese startup, is shipping flat-packed cardboard suicide drones at ~$2,000 per unit — modeled on the disposable FPV-drone economics proven by Ukraine and Hezbollah. Lead with the unit cost and the country: Japan, which constitutionally renounced offensive weapons in 1947, now has a domestic loitering-munition supplier. Frame this as the Tokyo half of the Russia's-9-May story — pacifism inversion is also a supply-chain story, and a flatpacked cardboard drone is the cheapest entry ticket to peer-rival warfare ever produced.

stories.label: Press freedom at lowest level in 25 years: RSF
stories.summary: Reporters Without Borders' 2026 index marks a 25-year low, citing Trump's 'systematic' attacks on US press and Saudi Arabia's 2025 execution of a journalist. Lead with the asymmetry: the country that tells others to defend press freedom and the country whose Crown Prince was implicated in Khashoggi's killing now appear together as primary deterioration cases. Frame this not as a ranking story but as evidence that the post-2000 norm of legal protection for journalists has broken down across democracies and autocracies alike.

stories.label: Zelenskyy responds to Putin's proposal to declare ceasefire on 9 May
stories.summary: Putin proposed a 3-day ceasefire timed to Russia's May 9 Victory Day parade; Zelenskyy ordered his team to contact the Trump administration for clarification rather than accept or reject directly. Lead with the choreography: the ceasefire is structured around Russia's domestic commemoration, not the war's military logic, and a scaled-back parade (no tanks on Red Square) signals just how depleted Russian heavy armour is. The mechanism worth highlighting — Kyiv now routes responses to Moscow through Washington, formalising US arbitration of the war's terms.

stories.label: Gaza's Medical Evacuation Crisis Is Leaving Thousands Without Care
stories.summary: Thousands of Gaza patients with cancer, kidney failure, and combat injuries are stranded because the Rafah crossing's medical evacuation pipeline has functionally collapsed under Israeli vetting and Egyptian capacity limits. Lead with the bottleneck mechanism — patients are not denied care by absence of doctors abroad but by approval queues that outlast the diseases. Continuation of siege IS the development; this is who bears the cost when 'ceasefire' is partial.

stories.label: Sindh education department to introduce religious textbooks for Hindu students
stories.summary: Sindh province will, for the first time, supply state-published Hindu religious-studies textbooks to Hindu students rather than forcing them into Islamiyat or unaccredited private materials. Lead with what this corrects: minority students in Pakistan have for decades been counted as 'Muslim by default' on assessments. The mechanism is mundane curriculum policy; the consequence is recognition that Pakistan's largest religious minority has standing in the public-school system, not just an opt-out.

stories.label: US Court Dismisses Rohingya Hate Speech Lawsuit Against Meta
stories.summary: A US federal court dismissed Rohingya refugees' $150B suit alleging Facebook's algorithm amplified the genocidal incitement that drove their 2017 expulsion from Myanmar. Lead with the legal mechanism — Section 230 plus extraterritoriality doctrine — and the precedent it sets: platforms cannot be sued in US courts for foreign harms even when their own internal documents acknowledge the role. The dignity question for the reader: where do Muslim minorities in the Global South go for redress when the platform is American and the genocide is somewhere else?

stories.label: Belgium in talks with Engie to nationalise country's nuclear assets
stories.summary: Belgium is buying its nuclear plants back from France's Engie and extending two reactors that were scheduled to shut, formally reversing a 2003 phase-out law. Lead with the reversal: a European country that legislated nuclear's end is now legislating its return, paying Engie to undo what Engie was paid to do. The mechanism worth highlighting — sovereignty over base-load power has become more valuable than market-driven energy policy after the 2022–24 gas crises, and France's Engie is now in the unusual position of selling nuclear assets back to host states rather than operating them.

stories.label: An old railroad is key to U.S.-China race for critical metals in Africa
stories.summary: The Lobito Corridor — a colonial-era Angolan railway being refurbished with US backing — is the physical chokepoint that will determine whether DRC and Zambian copper and cobalt move west to American buyers or stay on Chinese-controlled rails heading east. Lead with the infrastructure stakes: the US has committed hundreds of millions to one rail line because that single line is what 'reshoring' critical minerals actually means in practice. Frame for a reader who needs to understand that critical-minerals competition is not about contracts but about track gauges, ports, and which power maintains the route.

stories.label: Smog from wildfires increasingly harmful, data show
stories.summary: New epidemiological data show wildfire smog is becoming MORE toxic per microgram over time — not just more abundant — because the fires are now burning more synthetic materials (homes, cars, plastics) than vegetation. Lead with the per-particle finding: the standard PM2.5 dose-response curves clinicians use to assess risk are calibrated to old vegetation-fire chemistry and now systematically underestimate harm. The mechanism — urban-wildland interface fires release chlorinated and metallic compounds that traditional smoke didn't.

stories.label: Will Chinese megaprojects solve northern Peru's water crisis?
stories.summary: Chinese state firms are bidding to build trans-Andean water tunnels that would divert Amazon-basin runoff to Peru's parched Pacific coast — a hydrological inversion the Peruvian state has wanted for half a century but never financed. Lead with the trade-off: the megaproject would solve Lima-region drought while moving the deficit upstream onto Amazonian indigenous communities and biodiversity. The structural shift — Chinese capital is now financing the kind of nation-scale water infrastructure that Western development banks abandoned in the 1990s.

stories.label: Coupang probe tests the U.S.'s willingness to protect its tech giants abroad
stories.summary: South Korea's antitrust probe into Coupang — a US-listed Korean platform with Amazon-style market power — has triggered congressional pushback in Washington framing the investigation as protectionism against a US company. Lead with the inversion: the same arguments US trustbusters make against Amazon are being used by Korean regulators against Coupang, and Washington's response reveals that 'tech sovereignty' rhetoric only flows one way. The structural angle for the reader — antitrust law is becoming an arena where the US conditions trade preferences on a partner's willingness to spare American-listed platforms from local enforcement.

stories.label: Google's privacy maze: How Gemini traps you and your data
stories.summary: Ars Technica walks through the actual settings paths a Gemini user must traverse to prevent their prompts, file uploads, and Gmail context from training Google's models — and finds the controls split across three product surfaces with non-obvious defaults that re-enable on app updates. Lead with the specific dark-pattern mechanism: 'opting out' of Gemini training does not opt you out of human review of flagged conversations, which Google retains for up to three years regardless. The reader is a developer or knowledge worker whose company-data leakage risk depends on understanding this distinction.

stories.label: Crypto hacks continue as Wasabi Protocol drained for $4.5 million in admin key compromise
stories.summary: Wasabi Protocol lost $4.5M when an attacker obtained an admin key and called privileged functions on the protocol's smart contracts directly — not a code exploit, an access-control failure. Lead with the recurring DeFi pattern: the 'decentralised' protocol had a single multisig with the power to unilaterally drain user funds, and that multisig's private keys are the actual security boundary. The mechanism worth highlighting — most 2026 DeFi losses are now governance-key compromises rather than reentrancy bugs, which means the 'code is law' framing has been replaced by 'whoever holds the keys is law'.

stories.label: Russian Drones Strike Ukraine's Odesa Overnight, Wounding 18, Officials Say
stories.summary: Russian drones hit Odesa overnight, wounding 18 — striking homes, a kindergarten, a hotel and a shopping center. Lead with the civilian targets (kindergarten, hotel) and the 5-source convergence on damage scope; the structural angle is that drone-led strikes on Black Sea port cities continue irrespective of stated ceasefire diplomacy. Multi-source: US/Ukraine/Russia-exile/India/Türkiye.

stories.label: Vaishnaw flags off Jammu-Srinagar Vande Bharat, services from May 2
stories.summary: India inaugurates the first all-weather rail link to Kashmir Valley — Vande Bharat from Jammu (Katra) to Srinagar via the Chenab and Anji bridges. Lead with the engineering: this is the world's highest railway arch (359m) and a 272km route through 38 tunnels, integrating Kashmir into the national grid in a way road/air never could. The structural why: Delhi is binding J&K economically post-370, with a transport project that operates year-round through the Pir Panjal — every previous land link closed for months in winter.

stories.label: Supreme Court Says Minor Cannot Be Forced To Carry Pregnancy
stories.summary: India's Supreme Court ruled that a minor rape survivor cannot be compelled to continue a pregnancy beyond 24 weeks — and ordered Parliament to amend the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act for under-18 survivors. The structural reveal: the bench used Article 142 to direct legislative reform, a precedent-setting move on bodily autonomy in a country where the existing 24-week ceiling has stranded child rape survivors in court for years. Lead with the AIIMS case that triggered the ruling and the directive to amend the law.

stories.label: 5 Takeaways from 2025's Cocaine Seizure Data
stories.summary: InSight Crime's 2025 cocaine seizure data shows the trade is restructuring — Ecuador and Europe overtook traditional transit corridors, Colombia's production keeps climbing, and 'narco-submarines' in the Atlantic are now a routine intercept category. Lead with the Atlantic shift: the trafficking map that defined the 2010s (Caribbean → US) is being replaced by a Pacific-Ecuador-Antwerp pipeline. Structural angle for readers: enforcement frames this as a victory but seizure volume rising alongside production points to Plan Colombia's failure as a supply-side strategy.

stories.label: India's Bangladesh gamble
stories.summary: Delhi's bet that the post-Hasina interim government in Dhaka would remain pliant has collapsed — Bangladesh is rebuilding ties with Pakistan and warming to Beijing while transit access for India's northeast hangs in the balance. Lead with the concrete: stalled border-haat trade, the Teesta water deal frozen, and the strategic cost to India's 'Act East' policy. The structural angle: 15 years of Indian leverage built around one ruling party evaporated in a year — a lesson in regional power dependent on personal political alliances.

stories.label: Snow cover on Greek mountains has more than halved in four decades, study finds
stories.summary: A four-decade satellite analysis shows snow cover on Greek mountains has more than halved — with cascading consequences for summer water tables, hydropower, and the country's wildfire season. Lead with the headline number (>50% loss since the 1980s) and one downstream effect (Mornos reservoir, summer river flow, or fire-fuel moisture). Structural angle: Mediterranean snowpack is a rarely-discussed climate indicator, and Greece's loss prefigures what southern Spain, Italy and the Levant face — a regional water-system reorganization, not a one-country story.

stories.label: A 2022 Law May Be Quietly Helping People Stay on Their Meds
stories.summary: Early evidence suggests the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare drug-price provisions — capping insulin and out-of-pocket Part D costs — are improving medication adherence among older Americans. Lead with the adherence delta (insulin or cardiovascular drugs), the population affected, and the methodology limit (no controlled trial yet). Structural angle: this is rare US health policy where a law's mechanism (price cap → affordability → adherence → outcomes) is being measured at each step, and the early signal contradicts the pharma industry argument that price caps would harm patient access.

stories.label: Your phone is about to stop being yours
stories.summary: Google's developer-verification rollout will require all Android apps — including sideloaded APKs — to be signed by a Google-verified developer ID, eliminating anonymous distribution and the practical ability to install non-Play Store software on certified Android devices. Lead with the concrete change (the verification gate, the timeline, what breaks: F-Droid, modded apps, region-specific banking sideloads). Structural angle: the last general-purpose mobile OS is becoming app-store-gated; every banking, social, and surveillance-circumvention app on Android now requires Google's permission to exist. The reader is a developer or a user in a country where Play Store coverage is unreliable.

stories.label: Ghostty is leaving GitHub
stories.summary: Mitchell Hashimoto is moving the Ghostty terminal off GitHub, citing AI-scraping, automated low-quality issues, and Microsoft/GitHub's product direction. Lead with the why (the specific failure modes — bot-spam issues, Copilot training scraping without consent, opaque moderation) and the destination (self-hosted Forgejo). Structural angle: a marquee open-source project leaving the dominant code-host is a signal — the open-source/AI-scraping conflict is now severe enough that maintainers are paying the migration tax. Worth tracking which projects follow.

stories.label: Humanitarian aid turns to AI as crises outpace capacity
stories.summary: The IRC's Signpost service is using LLM-powered chatbots to triage refugee queries (asylum procedures, shelter, medical) at scale across Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine and Latin America — caseloads grew faster than caseworkers could be hired. Lead with the scale (queries served, languages, geographies) and one named failure mode (hallucinated legal advice, missed protection cases). Structural angle: humanitarian AI is happening because the funding gap is widening, not because the technology is ready — and the populations being experimented on have no realistic alternative.
